title: How did women live in the Viking Age?
sentences: So how can we even find out how women lived their lives in a
period that lasts roughly from the year eight hundred to the year ten fifty?
As an archaeologist I would say that especially in the early parts the archaeological material is
very important, and then the grave material is some of what shows us both women and men.
Because there we find these graves where you are dressed
in your costume and you've been given a lot of objects.
What characterises the burial custom of the Viking Age is that the
graves are so well equipped, so that gives us a picture.
And in addition we also have material from the textiles in the Oseberg grave,
small miniature figures that simply show us the people and how they looked.
And then of course there's this wealth of written sources,
which to a large extent is the view from outside, the view of those who
experience the Vikings, the raids, that is, the men of the church in particular.
And it's from outside in time too, medieval authors who recreate the stories of the Viking Age.
So to a large extent retrospective as well then, in the written sources, yes.
Simply put.
Yes.
What does it mean to relate primarily to the material sources, which
I assume you do first and foremost, that is, to the speech of things?
I imagine it gives a larger room for interpretation perhaps,
but that at the same time it's even harder than having to relate critically to written sources.
What do you think about that?
I think it gives an enormous opportunity to relate critically to written sources
because you see some of what the written sources don't tell, you see for example the breadth of roles,
you see all those
who are left out of written sources, and you see a diversity.
And of course there are many challenges in interpreting material culture,
but there are, after all, also with written sources.
We humans are very fond of editing and presenting ourselves
as we'd prefer, and that's what we see with the graves.
But the archaeological material also includes traces of activity, traces of
ritual, traces of everyday life, farms, buildings, the earliest towns.
And here we can kind of piece it together from many angles and also
bring in the written material, to put a large body of material into play.
So it doesn't only work as a supplement, but also as a correction in some cases.
